title: Appended statement by Attilio Macero on composition
summary: An unrelated statement by Attilio Macero about his compositions and combining jazz and classical elements is appended.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I also have one commercial recording to my credit which features my quintet and four of my original compositions. This is on the Debut label and came out this year. I have also within the past year appeared on several radio shows presenting some of my compositions. These were on W.O.V. and the most recent on W.N.Y.C. on their Adventures In Music program August 1954. At this time I am also negotiating with one of the large record companies to record several of my new compositions. All of this I believe has helped in this thing I believe in concerning the progress of music, since it gives me the opportunity to present my ideas to the listening public in both words and music. Through my efforts and those of others, will come, I hope, an acceptance by the public of a type of music that is unfamiliar to them.

I have not found a teacher of this particular type of hybrid music, but have certainly found sympathetic people in music who are making efforts along these same lines; such people as Peggy Glanville-Hicks, David Broekman, Henry Brant, William Schuman, and many more.

For several years I have been interested in composition but really did not start any serious writing until around 1948. At this time I minored in composition at the Juilliard School of Music until I completed my studies there in 1952. Following my graduation in 1952, I began studying composition privately with Henry Brant.

I have always been interested in jazz, since I have continually played with dance bands for about the last ten years. Then, at Juilliard, I had an opportunity to strengthen my classical, musical background. Sometime during this period I began to be dissatisfied with what was happening to our present day music and the direction, or rather, non-direction, it was taking. This is where I first began to experiment with the idea of combining the elements which I felt were the strongest of classical and jazz composition together to give us a more meaningful and progressive, if you will, type of expression. I surely do not feel that I have been entirely successful in this yet, but, like others, feel very strongly that it is something that needs to be done and that many worthwhile advances in music could come from such conscientious effort to improve our standard of composition.

To date I have written thirteen major works which have all been performed publically; most of them within the past year in New York City. Among these works are several collections of quartets, duets, and some short pieces for piano which have been performed in various music classes at the Juilliard School of Music.

I believe I should mention here also that while a student at Juilliard I organized and let a dance band that played for Juilliard functions such as dances, etc. This was done with the consent of the administration. We also played several times for the Bandstand U.S.A. show over radio W.O.R. and gave several benefit performances at local veterans and mental hospitals. This, of course, does not bear on my project, but does, I believe, add to my knowledge of the current danceband, music field.
